canonical_statement: The review sought to systematically evaluate L-methylfolate augmentation in adults with major depressive disorder and meta-analyze its efficacy.
Two reviewers independently searched PubMed for English-language articles through December 31, 2020, with manual bibliography searching and third-reviewer adjudication for disagreements.

Eligible articles examined adjunctive L-methylfolate in human depressive disorders or antidepressant response, were peer reviewed and English language, and had full text available; non-original research was excluded.

population.label: Human studies of depressive disorders or antidepressant response
inclusion_criteria: L-methylfolate adjunctive therapy or effect on antidepressant response
exclusion_criteria: Review articles, commentaries, books/book chapters, editorials, and other non-original research

canonical_statement: Meta-analyses were restricted to randomized controlled trials reporting HAM-D17 response or HAM-D17 scores at the trial endpoint.

The response meta-analysis used Mantel-Haenszel relative risks, and the continuous HAM-D17 meta-analysis used Hedges g standardized mean differences; 95% confidence intervals and alpha 0.05 were used.
For both meta-analytic outcomes, a sensitivity analysis removed the trial using 7.5 mg L-methylfolate to reduce dose-related variability.
Funnel plots and statistical publication-bias testing were not performed because fewer than 10 studies were available.
Risk of bias for the trials included in meta-analysis was assessed with the Cochrane risk of bias tool.
The review included 9 articles representing 10 studies; four studies contributed to the meta-analyses.
The PRISMA flow reports 816 records identified, 6 duplicates removed, 810 records screened, 17 full-text reports assessed, and 9 articles included.
The included evidence comprised four double-blind randomized controlled trials, three post-hoc reports from one trial cohort, one prospective naturalistic study, and two retrospective studies.
Across included studies, L-methylfolate was used at 7.5 or 15 mg/day.
Table 1 shows that most included study populations were middle-aged and predominantly women; all study participants were of European ancestry except the Kakar study population, which was East Asian.

population.label: Participants in the 10 studies summarized in Table 1

canonical_statement: Across three controlled trials (N=483), random-effects meta-analysis found greater HAM-D17 response with adjunctive L-methylfolate than with no L-methylfolate (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.08-1.46; p=0.004).

population.label: Adults with MDD in three controlled trials included in the HAM-D17 response meta-analysis

exposures.details: Adjunctive to antidepressant therapy; dose varied across included trials.

canonical_statement: A fixed-effects sensitivity model for HAM-D17 response remained statistically significant (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.07-1.48; p=0.005).

population.label: Adults with MDD in the controlled trials included in the HAM-D17 response meta-analysis

exposures.details: Adjunctive to antidepressant therapy; dose varied across included trials.

canonical_statement: After excluding the 7.5 mg trial, the two 15 mg trials did not show a statistically significant HAM-D17 response advantage (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.90-2.11; p=0.14).

population.label: Adults with MDD in the two 15 mg trials included in the HAM-D17 response sensitivity analysis

canonical_statement: Statistical heterogeneity for the three-trial HAM-D17 response meta-analysis was I2=0% (p=0.43), although the authors cautioned that clinical or methodological heterogeneity likely remained.
Across four trials (N=507), random-effects meta-analysis found lower endpoint HAM-D17 scores with adjunctive L-methylfolate (SMD -0.38, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.17; p=0.0003).

population.label: Adults with MDD in four controlled trials included in the endpoint HAM-D17 score meta-analysis

exposures.details: Adjunctive to antidepressant therapy; dose varied across included trials.

canonical_statement: The fixed-effects sensitivity model for endpoint HAM-D17 score also favored adjunctive L-methylfolate (SMD -0.39, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.21; p<0.0001).

population.label: Adults with MDD in four controlled trials included in the endpoint HAM-D17 score meta-analysis

exposures.details: Adjunctive to antidepressant therapy; dose varied across included trials.

canonical_statement: After excluding the 7.5 mg trial, the 15 mg-only endpoint HAM-D17 score analysis remained statistically significant (SMD -0.49, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.28; p<0.0001).

population.label: Adults with MDD in the three 15 mg trials included in the endpoint HAM-D17 score sensitivity analysis

canonical_statement: Statistical heterogeneity for the four-trial endpoint HAM-D17 score meta-analysis was low (I2=16%, p=0.31).
The review reports that Papakostas trial 1 (N=148) found no HAM-D17 efficacy difference between 7.5 mg L-methylfolate augmentation and placebo.
The review reports that Papakostas trial 2 (N=75) found greater HAM-D17 symptomatic improvement with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus SSRI than with SSRI plus placebo (-5.58 vs -3.04; p=0.05).

population.label: Adults with MDD and inadequate SSRI response in Papakostas trial 2

canonical_statement: The review reports HAM-D17 response rates of 32.3% with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus SSRI versus 14.6% with SSRI plus placebo in Papakostas trial 2 (p=0.04).

population.label: Adults with MDD and inadequate SSRI response in Papakostas trial 2

canonical_statement: Table 1 reports greater symptom improvement with L-methylfolate 7.5 or 15 mg plus SSRI/SNRI than with SSRI/SNRI alone in the Ginsberg 2011 retrospective study (N=242).

Table 1 reports a trend toward greater HAM-D17 reduction with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus psychotropic medication than with placebo plus psychotropic medication in Godfrey 1990 (24 depressed participants).
Table 1 reports better HAM-D17 response with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus escitalopram than with placebo plus escitalopram in Kakar 2017 (N=260).

Table 1 reports greater response with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus SSRI than with placebo plus SSRI in the Shelton 2015 post-hoc analysis, with inflammatory and obesity-related factors associated with response.
Table 1 reports improved response with 15 mg L-methylfolate plus SSRI versus placebo plus SSRI in Papakostas 2014 when patients were stratified by biological and genetic biomarkers.
The review reports that C677T and A1298C MTHFR variants were not significantly associated with L-methylfolate improvement or response in the included biomarker study.

The review reports that a retrospective registry study found better adherence and lower medical utilization and depression-related costs with adjunctive L-methylfolate than with second-generation antipsychotic augmentation.
The authors judged the studies included in the meta-analysis to have moderate to high risk of bias.
Adverse reactions were not meta-analyzed because the included trials provided insufficient adverse-event data, and number needed to harm could not be calculated.

The authors caution that the evidence may not generalize to all patients with MDD because most studied participants were women of European background in their 40s with inadequate response to multiple antidepressant trials.

The review could not determine whether particular SSRIs or SNRIs are better partners for L-methylfolate augmentation and identified no efficacy data for other antidepressant classes such as tricyclics.
The impact of MTHFR genetic variation on L-methylfolate efficacy remained inconclusive; only one small eligible adult study assessed this question.
The review did not perform meta-regression to adjust for methodological differences across studies because too few studies were available.
The systematic review and meta-analysis was restricted to adults with major depressive disorder, limiting inference to pediatric or bipolar populations.
The time course of response and the optimal stage at which to add L-methylfolate remained unclear.
The authors conclude that adjunctive L-methylfolate may have modest efficacy in antidepressant-treated adults with major depressive disorder.
The authors state that the study did not receive funding.
The conflict-of-interest statement reports that LCB was an employee of Tempus Labs, which provides MTHFR genetic testing, and lists professional-network memberships for several authors.
